newsitem.title: USA: Prospects for US 10-year sale downgraded to "OK".
newsitem.headline: Prospects for US 10-year sale downgraded to "OK".

text.p: A small U.S. Treasury market rally in the morning may have hurt the chances for a very successful 10-year note auction Wednesday afternoon, market players warned, even tough the U.S. Treasury market was chomping at the bit for new 10-year notes just two days ago.
Around noon EDT, the when-issued 10-year note was bid at 6.195 percent, below the crucial 6.20-percent level that market said was crucial to generate substantial bidding from retail accounts.

"We are getting up to levels where they are unattractive to certain accounts," said Jim Stewart, senior trader at Yamaichi International (America) Inc. "People wanted to buy at 6.25, 6.26 percent." He warned that if the yield stays below 6.20 percent, "we will lose the bigger bids."

Unless the bottom falls out of the market, a 6.25 percent yield looks like a pipe-dream for the $12.0 billion offering. "We may bo back up, but not to 6.25," said Neil DeSarno, head government bond trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "But we still have an hour left and a lot can happen."
Lower-than-usual volume of around $1 billion at midday was behind some of the uncertainty regarding prospects for the note sale.

The thin activity resulted in one buyer, said to have bought a block of when-issued 10s, being able to push the market below 6.20 percent. So, 6.20 percent appeared to be the new threshhold -- and wish -- for the 10-year's success.
The most likely scenario, traders said, would be for the auction to be Street-driven, leaving retail to buy the new supply from the dealers.
"But it will be tough getting any follow-through because (Thursday's) 30-year bond auction will put a cap on it," said a 10-year note trader at a leading primary dealership.

Traders noted that the market was in much better shape to digest the new notes Wednesday than it was late last week, thanks to Friday's huge selloff that pushed yields about 18 to 20 basis points higher.
"We got the correction we hoped for," DeSarno said. "The market still has a bullish tone and we look at this correction and say, 'this auction is going to go OK.'"
